unverified: DISTRICTS: Ohio Secretary of State pages and district PDFs returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so no official SOS lookup was opened. Districts (Congress 15, Ohio Senate 15, Ohio House 1) come from the U.S. Census Bureau geocoder run on the Statehouse's public coordinates (https://geocoding.geo.census.gov/geocoder/geographies/coordinates?x=-83.0003&y=39.9611&benchmark=Public_AR_Current&vintage=Current_Current&layers=all&format=json). The Ohio House 1 result is consistent with Rep. Jarrells' official House page (District 1, Columbus) but that page does not prove the building's district. Congressional District 15 is UNVERIFIED by an Ohio-source map: nearby points return District 3 and District 15, so the building sits in a boundary area. Confirm with the Franklin County sample ballot generator at https://vote.franklincountyohio.gov.

Columbus voters in some precincts also get precinct-level liquor local-option questions (#10A through #17b on the certified list). Whether any applies to the Statehouse precinct is UNVERIFIED; the certified questions list was revised 9/4/2026 (pages marked 9/1 and 9/4), after which the Board may revise it again.

Judicial pairings: the Common Pleas General and Domestic Relations, and Court of Appeals seats are listed above as separate UNCONTESTED seats because each candidate has a different term-commencing date on the Franklin County list. No second source (campaign page or court roster) was found for these pairings. The Probate seat (Green, Junga, same date) is corroborated by Columbus Bar Association profiles for both.

Write-in column: the PDF header is garbled ('DWrite-In'). Candidates with party 'N/A' and 'Yes' in that column are treated as declared write-ins. Gary Josephson (U.S. House 15) and Greg Levy (U.S. Senate, 'Other-party c') show no such flag and are listed as printed candidates; this reading is UNVERIFIED.

Whether Issue 8 or Issue 9 prevails if both pass: one news outlet (Axios, not opened, search snippet only) says the charter gives the win to the issue with more votes; the 8/24/2026 council ordinance text was not opened. UNVERIFIED.

Ohio House 1 incumbent's press release on a 'Gas Tax Holiday Act' (HB 1019, House vote 78-16) could not be matched: the legislature.ohio.gov HB 1019 page shows no votes recorded. Left out of evidence.
Campaign finance for Governor is secondhand (Signal Ohio and NBC4 reports of official filings); the Ohio Secretary of State finance site was blocked (HTTP 403).
Passage threshold and turnout conditions for Issue 3 and Issues 8/9 were not checked in an official source.

Probate Court: Kelly Green's current title (Chief Magistrate) is supported by her Columbus Bar Association profile only; the court's staff page (probate.franklincountyohio.gov) returned HTTP 403. UNVERIFIED by the court.

races.summary: Three tickets are printed on the ballot: Amy Acton and David Pepper, Don Kissick and James L. Mills, and Vivek Ramaswamy and Robert A. McColley.
races.turns_on: Which ticket's stated plans on taxes, schools, public safety and government a voter prefers, and how much weight to give each background: Acton's pandemic-era health agency record, Ramaswamy's business and short federal advisory role, and Kissick's campaign platform (no record or finance data found); no candidate has held elected office.

options.name: Amy Acton (Democratic), running with David Pepper

evidence.text: As Ohio Department of Health director she issued or recommended the state's early COVID-19 orders (fitness-festival spectator ban March 4, 2020; statewide school closure within a week; cancellation of in-person voting on the March 17, 2020 primary day). She left the post June 11, 2020 and stayed on as an adviser to Gov. DeWine. Orders drew lawsuits and a House effort to limit her authority (AP via News4JAX).

Campaign page (viewed 2026-10-06, undated) proposes an Ohio earned income credit and a child tax credit of $1,000 per child ages 0-6 and $500 ages 7-18 for families earning up to $85,000; the page cites about 775,000 families and 1.4 million children.

Campaign page (viewed 2026-10-06, undated) proposes restoring public school funding to a constitutional level and implementing the Fair School Funding Plan, redirecting voucher money to public schools with more accountability, and free school breakfast and lunch.

Campaign page (viewed 2026-10-06, undated) proposes a state 'Ohio Rx' drug-purchasing platform using Medicaid purchasing power, counting out-of-pocket drug costs toward deductibles, and state purchase of medical debt for relief.

Signal Ohio (June 19, 2026), reporting the filing for April 16 to June 12, 2026: Acton raised $10.6 million in 2026 and held $8.1 million cash on hand. Secondhand; official Ohio SOS filing not opened.

options.name: Don Kissick (Libertarian), running with James L. Mills

evidence.text: Campaign page (viewed 2026-10-06, undated) supports ending property taxes in favor of 'local consumption based funding' and eliminating corporate subsidies to balance budgets.

Campaign page proposes a five-year ban on legislators becoming lobbyists after leaving office, ending corporate contributions from regulated industries, and public searchable databases of government contracts.
Campaign page opposes data-center development on farmland and seeks to end special tax incentives for data centers.
Campaign page opposes automated license-plate camera networks and vehicle-tracking databases and calls for limits on mass-surveillance systems.

options.name: Vivek Ramaswamy (Republican), running with Robert A. McColley

evidence.text: Named in November 2024 with Elon Musk to lead the advisory Department of Government Efficiency; left in January 2025 after saying he planned to run for governor (reported by WSET/ABC News). He has not held elected office. No state record to cite.

Campaign plan page (viewed 2026-10-06, undated): 'slash property taxes immediately,' eliminate capital gains taxes, phase out the state income tax, and gas-tax relief; data-center tax revenue to fund homeowner rebates.

Campaign plan page proposes literacy (3rd grade), numeracy (8th grade) and civics (12th grade) standards, more parent choice over where children learn, higher pay for top-performing teachers, and expanded career-technical programs.

Campaign plan page proposes stricter bail and sentencing for repeat violent offenders, support for local law enforcement capacity, and addressing severe psychiatric illness to redirect police resources.

Signal Ohio (June 19, 2026), reporting the filing for April 16 to June 12, 2026: Ramaswamy raised $9.6 million in 2026 and held $26.8 million cash on hand, including a $25 million personal loan made in 2025. Secondhand; official Ohio SOS filing not opened.

races.summary: The ballot lists an incumbent House member and a first-time legislative candidate for a district covering downtown Columbus per Census Bureau data (see unverified).
races.turns_on: Whether a voter weighs the incumbent's documented legislative votes and sponsored bills against the challenger's business background and stated priorities, which have little legislative record to compare.

evidence.text: Primary sponsor with Rep. Josh Williams of H.B. 57 (overdose-reversal medication in schools). House passed 96-0 on 5-7-2025; Senate passed 28-4 on 10-1-2025; the vote page also lists a House passage vote of 76-18 on 10-1-2025.
Voted no on Senate Joint Resolution 10 (photo ID constitutional amendment, now State Issue 3) when the House adopted it 62-30 on 6-10-2026 (Ohio Legislature roll call).

Campaign page (undated) lists bills he says he co-authored, including H.B. 69 (minimum wage to $15), H.B. 274 (local firearm regulation), H.B. 367 (police body cameras) and H.B. 114 (Poindexter Village historic site). Bill outcomes not checked.
Official House page lists him as the District 1 member from Columbus with a stated priority of high-paying careers, quality education and safety from firearms.
BallotReady profile (aggregator, candidate-supplied, undated): says rents, utilities and food costs are rising faster than income, and supports entrepreneurship and fiscal accountability.
BallotReady profile (aggregator, candidate-supplied, undated): says schools should exceed state standards, with priorities in financial literacy, technology education and skilled trades.

BallotReady profile: CEO and managing partner of Shareatech.com; MBA, Franklin University; B.S. in Actuarial Science, Ohio State (1984). No legislative record found; the campaign homepage votegreff.com lists no issue positions.

races.race: Judge of the Court of Common Pleas, Probate Division (Franklin County)
races.summary: Two candidates are listed for the probate judgeship, which handles estates, guardianships, adoptions and civil commitments and whose judge also serves as clerk of the court.
races.turns_on: Whether a voter prefers a candidate whose experience is inside the Probate Court as a magistrate or one whose experience is as a trial and public-defender attorney; both bios are candidate-supplied.

evidence.text: Columbus Bar Association profile (candidate-supplied): Chief Magistrate, Franklin County Probate Court (2021-present); General Magistrate (2010-2021); staff attorney, Franklin County Common Pleas General Division (2002-2010). The court's own staff page could not be opened, so her current title is UNVERIFIED by the court.

Columbus Bar Association candidate profile statement: she says the Probate Judge also serves as clerk and so leads court operations as well as deciding cases, and cites teaching judges, magistrates and attorneys across Ohio.

Campaign site (undated) lists court changes and priorities: improving technology and simplifying processes, staff diversity and equal pay, and expanded free legal resources for the public; no endorsements listed.

Columbus Bar Association profile (candidate-supplied, not independently confirmed): 25+ years as an attorney, more than 100 jury trials as lead counsel, 12 years at the Franklin County Public Defender's Office, Director of the Ross County Office of the Ohio Public Defender, and Interim Chief Public Defender in Delaware County; certified for capital defense.

Columbus Bar Association candidate profile statement: he says a Probate Judge must also manage a branch of county government that is accessible, efficient and responsive, and cites budget oversight of up to $2 million in public defender offices.
Campaign site (undated) says a judge should be accessible, responsive, respectful and connected to the community and emphasizes efficiency in courtrooms; no endorsements listed.

races.race: State Issue 3: Require voters to present photo identification
races.summary: A General Assembly-initiated constitutional amendment that writes a photo ID requirement for voting into the Ohio Constitution.
races.turns_on: Whether placing an existing statutory ID requirement in the Constitution (harder to change later) is worth it, and whether the ID types and the mail-voting rule it specifies are the right ones.
races.yes_means: Adds Section 5 to Article V: in-person voters must show an unexpired Ohio driver's license or state ID, U.S. passport or card, or military, Ohio National Guard or VA ID; the law may offer an alternative for a sincere religious objection; other voting methods need photo ID or, if law allows, a signature plus another unique identifier; effective immediately. Source: https://search-prod.lis.state.oh.us/api/v2/general_assembly_136/legislation/sjr10/05_EN/pdf/
races.no_means: Photo ID stays a state statute (H.B. 458, signed January 6, 2023, in effect April 6, 2023), which the General Assembly can change by law. Source: https://ballotpedia.org/Ohio_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment_(2026)
races.fiscal: No official fiscal estimate found (the Secretary of State's Issue 3 report returned HTTP 403). The Ohio Controlling Board approved the Secretary of State's request for county newspaper notices of the amendment and arguments (more than $300,000, per WKBN; the request was $388,002): https://www.wkbn.com/news/elections/ohio-approves-money-to-educate-on-voter-id-amendment-2/amp/

for.text: House Speaker Matt Huffman says photo ID is overwhelmingly popular and routine for ordinary transactions; Rep. Adam Bird says it gives voters a chance to protect free and fair elections (Ballotpedia).

against.text: Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn says the ID rule is already law and the amendment will not change anyone's life; ACLU of Ohio's Gary Daniels says voter fraud is extremely rare and voting keeps getting harder (Ballotpedia).

evidence.text: Full text of Sub. S.J.R. 10 as sent to voters: new Article V, Section 5 (A) in-person photo ID, (B) other methods need photo ID or a signature plus unique identifier if authorized, (C) defines photo ID and unique identifier; effective on approval.
Senate adopted S.J.R. 10 22-9 on 6-3-2026 and the House adopted it 62-30 on 6-10-2026 (Ohio Legislature vote page); the resolution needed three-fifths of each chamber.

Ohio Controlling Board approved the Secretary of State's request (more than $300,000, per WKBN) as an emergency expense for county newspaper notices of the amendment and arguments; Sen. Catherine Ingram questioned whether newspapers reach underserved voters.

Supporters listed by Ballotpedia include President Trump, Sens. Gavarone, McColley, Timken, Reps. Bird and Huffman, and gubernatorial candidates Acton and Ramaswamy; opponents include Sens. Blackshear and Smith, Reps. Isaacsohn, Russo and Sims, gubernatorial candidate Kissick, ACLU of Ohio and Common Cause Ohio.
As of October 2026 Ballotpedia had not identified ballot-measure committees registered to support or oppose the amendment; it shows $0 reported on both sides.

races.race: Columbus Issues 8 and 9: charter amendments on how City Council is elected
races.summary: Two proposed Columbus charter amendments would both limit council voting to residents of each district; Issue 9 also adds four at-large seats over two cycles.
races.turns_on: Whether a voter wants district-only voting on the existing nine seats (Issue 8), a larger 13-member council with four at-large seats and a new map (Issue 9), or one of them only; how the two interact if both pass is unresolved in the sources found.
races.yes_means: Issue 8 (petition): only electors living in a district vote for or recall that district's council member; council stays at nine seats; ballots show citywide races plus the district race. Issue 9 (Council): the same district-only voting, plus two at-large seats elected in 2027 (seated 2028) and two more elected in 2029 (seated 2030), council growing from 9 to 11 to 13, a district map redraw in 2027 with allowed population variance rising from 1% to 7.5%, one-year district residency, and higher vote thresholds for some council actions. Sources: https://vote.franklincountyohio.gov/getmedia/a7a2dd78-e53f-4e74-933a-0ba0de9aaa4c/8-Full-OCOS-Charter-Amendment and https://vote.franklincountyohio.gov/getmedia/a3d9d75e-83ff-492a-98c4-a8cc09e1cd60/Notice-of-Election-Columbus-Charter-Amendment-2-Council
races.no_means: Council members continue to be elected citywide while living in one of nine districts (WOSU describes the current system as candidates who live in a district but must win a citywide majority). Source: https://www.wosu.org/politics-government/2026-03-04/columbus-voters-may-see-dueling-ballot-issues-to-change-the-city-councils-hybrid-district-system
races.fiscal: No official cost estimate for either amendment was found; the 8/24/2026 ordinance and fiscal documents were not opened. Cost of added council seats UNVERIFIED.

for.text: Our City, Our Say's Will Petrick says changing how council is elected will bring more responsiveness and accountability; Council President Shannon Hardin says a growing city needs to give more people a seat at the table (ABC6).

against.text: No organized opposition to the measures as printed was found. About the earlier petition drive only (WOSU, March 2026, before either measure was final): Jonathan Beard, who backed a separate district-only proposal with a new map, said the petition version ignored Black Columbus interests.

options.name: YES (Issue 8 and Issue 9 summarized together; vote separately)

evidence.text: Columbus City Council voted 8-0 on August 24, 2026 to place the petition amendment (Issue 8) on the November ballot and 8-0 to place its own amendment (Issue 9), per ABC6.
Issue 8 full text (Franklin County BOE): amends Charter Secs. 3, 4, 5 and 46 so council members are elected and recalled only by electors of their own district.

Issue 9 notice of election (Franklin County BOE, dated 9/14/2026): adds at-large seats, redraws map in 2027, 150-signature district and 250-signature at-large petition thresholds, 15% recall threshold by district or citywide.
WOSU (8/24/2026) reports Council President Shannon Hardin and Council member Rob Dorans said they would support both amendments in November; Dorans said the two ideas complement one another.

Kwesi Low (Columbus Stand Up) argued district-only voting would give districts leaders attentive to their challenges and cut campaign costs; Jonathan Beard criticized the petition drive's version (March 2026, before the final measures) as ignoring Black Columbus interests.
No campaign-finance totals for committees supporting or opposing Issue 8 or 9 were found in the sources opened.

gaps: Ohio Secretary of State pages (candidate lists, Issue 3 Ballot Board report with official YES/NO arguments, campaign finance site, district maps) blocked automated access with HTTP 403; official YES/NO arguments and fiscal analysis for Issue 3 could not be read.
Campaign finance: no state-level filings opened for Governor, House 1 or Probate; Governor totals are news reports of the filings.
Kissick: no record, no finance data, and no second source beyond his campaign site found.
Greff: no legislative or office record; only aggregator and campaign-homepage statements.

Green and Junga: experience claims rest on Columbus Bar Association profiles supplied by the candidates, including Green's current title (the probate court's page returned HTTP 403); no bar ratings, reversals or conduct findings were checked.
Columbus Issues 8 and 9: no official fiscal estimate, no committee funding, and no confirmation of the conflict rule if both pass.
Other statewide offices and Congress, Senate and Supreme Court races are listed but not researched (scope limit of 5 items).
